topics.name: William Lloyd Garrison
topics.kicker: Abolitionist editor of _The Liberator_ · Demanded an immediate end to slavery
topics.briefing: William Lloyd Garrison was a printer from Massachusetts who launched a Boston newspaper, _The Liberator_, on January 1, 1831, promising readers, “I will be heard.” He demanded an immediate end to slavery and helped found the American Anti-Slavery Society in 1833. In 1835 a Boston mob that hated his message dragged him through the streets with a rope, and on July 4, 1854, he burned a copy of the U.S. Constitution because it protected slavery.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: While working in Baltimore on Benjamin Lundy’s newspaper _Genius of Universal Emancipation_, this man was convicted of libel for attacking Francis Todd, a shipowner from his hometown whose ship had carried enslaved people for sale. He sat in jail for weeks until the New York merchant Arthur Tappan paid his fine.
tossups.r: The next year, he started his own newspaper in Boston. For 10 points, name this abolitionist who published _The Liberator_.

tossups.p: In the first issue of his weekly newspaper, this man promised readers that he would be “as harsh as truth, and as uncompromising as justice.” He went on, “I will not equivocate—I will not excuse—I will not retreat a single inch.”
tossups.r: He ended that passage with the words “and I will be heard.” For 10 points, name this Boston editor whose paper, _The Liberator_, first appeared on January 1, 1831.

tossups.p: At an 1854 Fourth of July rally in Framingham, Massachusetts, where Henry David Thoreau gave his speech “Slavery in Massachusetts,” this man burned a copy of the Fugitive Slave Act and the ruling that had sent Anthony Burns back to slavery.
tossups.r: He then burned the Constitution itself, crying, “So perish all compromises with tyranny!” For 10 points, name this abolitionist who published _The Liberator_.

tossups.p: In October 1835, a crowd hunting for the British abolitionist George Thompson broke up a meeting of the Boston Female Anti-Slavery Society and seized this man instead. Mayor Theodore Lyman had him locked in jail overnight to protect him from the mob.
tossups.r: The crowd had dragged him through the streets with a rope. For 10 points, name this Boston editor of _The Liberator_.

tossups.p: This man wrote the Declaration of Sentiments for a national group founded in Philadelphia in 1833, which rejected violence as a way to end slavery. In 1832, he had helped start the New England Anti-Slavery Society in Boston.
tossups.r: The 1833 group was the American Anti-Slavery Society. For 10 points, name this abolitionist who edited _The Liberator_.

tossups.p: When the World Anti-Slavery Convention in London refused to seat women delegates in 1840, this American arrived late and protested by sitting in the gallery with the women instead of taking his own seat.
tossups.r: That same year, his support for women’s leadership split the American Anti-Slavery Society. For 10 points, name this Boston abolitionist who published _The Liberator_.

tossups.p: The wealthy Black sailmaker James Forten helped pay for this man’s newspaper, and Black readers made up most of its first subscribers. This man’s 1832 book _Thoughts on African Colonization_ attacked the plan to send free Black Americans to Liberia.
tossups.r: He had once supported that plan himself. For 10 points, name this abolitionist who founded _The Liberator_ in 1831.

tossups.p: Georgia’s legislature offered a $5,000 reward to anyone who would arrest this man and bring him to trial in that state. Some Southern leaders blamed his newspaper for Nat Turner’s 1831 revolt in Virginia, though no evidence tied the two together.
tossups.r: That newspaper demanded an immediate end to slavery. For 10 points, name this editor of _The Liberator_.

tossups.p: This editor wrote the preface to an 1845 _Narrative_ by a man he had first heard speak at an antislavery meeting on Nantucket in 1841. The two men later split after the younger one decided that the Constitution could be used against slavery.
tossups.r: That younger man was Frederick Douglass. For 10 points, name this white abolitionist who founded _The Liberator_.

tossups.p: In 1838, this pacifist helped found the New England Non-Resistance Society, which rejected all use of force, even by governments. He refused to vote, believing that taking part in elections meant supporting a government that protected slavery.
tossups.r: He demanded the immediate freeing of all enslaved people. For 10 points, name this radical Boston abolitionist who published _The Liberator_.

tossups.p: Borrowing words from the Book of Isaiah, this man called the U.S. Constitution “a covenant with death, and an agreement with hell” because it protected slavery. He wanted the free states to break away from the slave states, under the slogan “No Union with Slaveholders.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this abolitionist who began publishing _The Liberator_ in Boston in 1831.

tossups.p: In April 1865, this man was an invited guest, along with the speaker Henry Ward Beecher, when Robert Anderson raised the U.S. flag again over Fort Sumter, four years after Confederates had captured the fort.
tossups.r: That December, after the Thirteenth Amendment ended slavery, he printed the last issue of his newspaper. For 10 points, name this abolitionist who founded _The Liberator_ in 1831.

tossups.p: As a young newspaper editor in his hometown of Newburyport, Massachusetts, this man published the first poem by John Greenleaf Whittier, who later joined the fight against slavery. He then edited a temperance paper in Boston before joining Benjamin Lundy in Baltimore.
tossups.r: He had learned his trade as a printer’s apprentice. For 10 points, name this abolitionist who later founded _The Liberator_.

tossups.p: This man and the printer Isaac Knapp started a weekly whose masthead declared, “Our country is the world—our countrymen are all mankind.” That paper ran for 35 years, though it never had more than a few thousand subscribers.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Boston editor of _The Liberator_, which first appeared in 1831.

tossups.p: In 1864, this man broke with his longtime ally Wendell Phillips by supporting Abraham Lincoln’s reelection. The next year, he stepped down as president of the American Anti-Slavery Society after proposing that the group shut down, and Phillips took over.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this abolitionist who had started the Boston newspaper _The Liberator_ in 1831.

trap.title: The man, not the movement
trap.body: This man is so closely tied to the antislavery cause that players sometimes blurt out “abolitionism” or the name of his newspaper instead of his name. Other abolitionist editors share his clues too: Frederick Douglass founded _The North Star_ after escaping slavery, and Elijah Lovejoy was an editor killed by a proslavery mob in Alton, Illinois, in 1837.
trap.fix: Listen for “this man” or “this editor.” _The Liberator_, “I will be heard,” the Boston mob of 1835, and burning the Constitution in 1854 all mean him. Rochester and escaping slavery mean Douglass; Alton, Illinois, means Lovejoy; “this movement” wants abolitionism.

topics.name: William McKinley
topics.kicker: 25th U.S. President · Led the nation in the Spanish-American War; shot in 1901
topics.briefing: William McKinley was the last Civil War veteran to become president; at Antietam, the teenage sergeant carried hot coffee and food to soldiers under fire. As the 25th president, he won the 1896 election by campaigning from his front porch in Canton, Ohio, led the country through the Spanish-American War, and annexed Hawaii. In September 1901, the anarchist Leon Czolgosz shot him at the Pan-American Exposition in Buffalo, New York, and Theodore Roosevelt became president.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: During the Battle of Antietam, this teenage commissary sergeant drove a wagon of hot coffee and food to Ohio soldiers under fire, and a monument on the battlefield honors him. His regiment had been led for a time by another future president, Rutherford B. Hayes.
tossups.r: He later became the last Civil War veteran elected president. For 10 points, name this president who led the nation in the Spanish-American War.

tossups.p: As chairman of the House Ways and Means Committee, this congressman wrote an 1890 law that sharply raised tariffs on imported goods, and he lost his House seat in elections later that year. He then served two terms as governor of Ohio.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Republican who won the presidency in 1896 by defeating William Jennings Bryan.

tossups.p: While his opponent traveled about 18,000 miles by train giving speeches in favor of “free silver,” this candidate stayed home in Canton, Ohio. Trains brought hundreds of thousands of visitors to hear him speak from his front porch.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Republican who defeated William Jennings Bryan in the 1896 presidential election.

tossups.p: The Cleveland industrialist Mark Hanna managed this man’s first presidential campaign, which defended the gold standard and raised huge sums from big businesses. Four years later, this man ran for reelection on the slogan “four more years of the full dinner pail.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Republican president who defeated William Jennings Bryan in 1896 and 1900.

tossups.p: Soon after taking office, this president called Congress into a special session that passed the Dingley Tariff, raising taxes on imports. In 1900, he signed the Gold Standard Act, which made gold the only standard for redeeming paper money.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Republican president who had defeated the free-silver champion William Jennings Bryan.

tossups.p: The Spanish diplomat Enrique Dupuy de Lôme [“doo-PWEE duh LOHM”] resigned after a New York newspaper printed his stolen letter calling this president “weak.” Days later, the USS _Maine_ exploded in Havana Harbor.
tossups.r: In April 1898, this president asked Congress to declare war on Spain. For 10 points, name this president during the Spanish-American War.

tossups.p: Mark Twain and Andrew Carnegie joined the Anti-Imperialist League to oppose this president’s decision to keep the Philippines. In 1899, the Senate approved his peace treaty with Spain by just one vote more than it needed.
tossups.r: That treaty gave the U.S. Puerto Rico, Guam, and the Philippines. For 10 points, name this president during the Spanish-American War.

tossups.p: Five years after American businessmen and planters overthrew Queen Liliuokalani [“lih-lee-oo-oh-kuh-LAH-nee”], this president signed the Newlands Resolution, annexing the islands she had ruled. Grover Cleveland had withdrawn an earlier treaty to take over those islands.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this president who annexed Hawaii in 1898, the same year he led the nation into war with Spain.

tossups.p: On the morning of September 6, 1901, this president toured Niagara Falls. That afternoon, he was shaking hands with a line of visitors in the Temple of Music, a concert hall at a world’s fair, when he was attacked; he died eight days later.
tossups.r: That fair was the Pan-American Exposition in Buffalo, New York, and the shooter was Leon Czolgosz [“CHOLE-gosh”]. For 10 points, name this 25th president.

tossups.p: The day before he was shot, this president told a huge crowd at a world’s fair that the United States could no longer stay isolated and should sign trade agreements with other nations. After his death, the Secret Service began protecting presidents full-time.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this president who was assassinated in Buffalo, New York, in 1901.

tossups.p: Ohio made the scarlet carnation its state flower in memory of this man, who often wore a red carnation for good luck. In the 1890s, a gold prospector named North America’s tallest peak after him.
tossups.r: That peak was renamed Denali in 2015, but a 2025 executive order restored his name to it for federal use. For 10 points, name this 25th president.

tossups.p: This president’s first vice president, Garret Hobart, a lawyer from Paterson, New Jersey, died in office in November 1899, and the vice presidency stayed empty for the rest of the term.
tossups.r: In 1900, the Republicans chose a new running mate, the Rough Rider Theodore Roosevelt. For 10 points, name this president, whom Roosevelt succeeded in 1901.

tossups.p: This president’s secretary of state, John Hay, sent the Open Door Notes asking other powers to give all nations equal trading rights in China. In 1900, this president sent American troops to help end the Boxer Rebellion’s siege of foreign diplomats in Beijing.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this president who led the nation in the Spanish-American War.

tossups.p: This president’s portrait appeared on the $500 bill, and he is buried with his wife, Ida, and their two daughters, who died young, in a domed memorial in Canton, Ohio. He was born in Niles, Ohio, in 1843.
tossups.r: He was assassinated in 1901. For 10 points, name this Republican, the 25th president of the United States.

tossups.p: In December 1898, this president issued a proclamation of “benevolent assimilation” for the Philippines. Weeks later, fighting broke out between American troops and Filipino forces led by Emilio Aguinaldo [“ah-ghee-NAHL-doh”], who wanted independence.
tossups.r: That conflict became the Philippine-American War. For 10 points, name this president who also annexed Hawaii and won the Spanish-American War.

trap.title: McKinley or Roosevelt?
trap.body: Theodore Roosevelt was McKinley’s assistant secretary of the Navy, then his vice president, and he became president when McKinley was shot, so their clues overlap: 1898, Cuba, and 1901. Players also blurt out William Jennings Bryan, the man McKinley beat twice, or Benjamin Harrison, the president who signed the 1890 tariff that McKinley wrote.
trap.fix: Who was shot in Buffalo, who campaigned from his front porch, and who asked Congress to declare war on Spain? McKinley. Who charged up San Juan Hill with the Rough Riders or took over in 1901? Roosevelt. Who gave the “Cross of Gold” speech and lost? Bryan.

topics.name: Wyoming
topics.kicker: Least populous U.S. state · First territory to let women vote (1869)
topics.briefing: Wyoming has fewer people than any other state, but it holds some big firsts. In 1869 its territorial legislature gave women the right to vote, earning it the nickname “the Equality State,” and in 1925 Nellie Tayloe Ross became the first woman governor in U.S. history. Most of Yellowstone, the world’s first national park, lies in its northwest corner, and Devils Tower became the first national monument in 1906.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1870, Esther Hobart Morris of South Pass City became the first woman in the United States to serve as a justice of the peace, in this territory. Just months earlier, its governor had signed a bill introduced by William Bright.
tossups.r: That 1869 law made it the first U.S. territory to let women vote. For 10 points, name this “Equality State.”

tossups.p: After her husband died in office, Nellie Tayloe Ross won a special election and took office in January 1925, about two weeks before Texas swore in Miriam “Ma” Ferguson. Ross later directed the U.S. Mint for twenty years.
tossups.r: Ross was the first woman governor in U.S. history. For 10 points, name the state she led, whose capital is Cheyenne.

tossups.p: The Teton Range towers over the valley of Jackson Hole in this state, where John D. Rockefeller Jr. secretly bought land in the 1920s and later donated it to expand Grand Teton National Park.
tossups.r: Old Faithful geyser erupts in another park in this state’s northwest corner. For 10 points, name this state that holds most of Yellowstone National Park.

tossups.p: Many Plains nations call a giant rock tower in this state “Bear Lodge,” and Steven Spielberg’s 1977 film _Close Encounters of the Third Kind_ ends there. Theodore Roosevelt made that tower the first national monument in 1906.
tossups.r: It is Devils Tower. For 10 points, name this state whose capital is Cheyenne.

tossups.p: Interior Secretary Albert Fall leased a federal oil reserve in this state to Harry Sinclair’s company in 1922 without competitive bidding. Fall was later convicted of taking a bribe and became the first former cabinet member sent to prison for crimes committed in office.
tossups.r: That reserve was named for a rock shaped like a teapot. For 10 points, name this state, the site of the Teapot Dome scandal.

tossups.p: Railroad surveyors founded this state’s capital in 1867 as a stop on the Union Pacific line and named it for a Plains Indian nation. That city holds Frontier Days, one of the world’s largest outdoor rodeos, every July.
tossups.r: That city is Cheyenne. For 10 points, name this state, the least populous in the nation.

tossups.p: Dick Cheney held this state’s only seat in the U.S. House from 1979 to 1989, and his daughter, Liz Cheney, held that same at-large seat from 2017 to 2023. This state has never had more than one House seat.
tossups.r: It has the smallest population of any state. For 10 points, name this state whose capital is Cheyenne.

tossups.p: Pioneers carved their names into Independence Rock, the “Register of the Desert,” as they crossed this state, and they hoped to reach that rock by the Fourth of July. Farther west, they crossed the Continental Divide at the wide, gentle South Pass.
tossups.r: That route was the Oregon Trail. For 10 points, name this state whose northwest corner holds most of Yellowstone National Park.

tossups.p: In December 1866, Lakota and Cheyenne warriors defeated William Fetterman’s soldiers near Fort Phil Kearny, in what is now this state, during Red Cloud’s War. That war ended in 1868 with a treaty signed at Fort Laramie, which also lies in this state.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Rocky Mountain state whose capital shares its name with one of those nations.

tossups.p: When Congress debated admitting this territory as a state, its lawmakers reportedly sent word that they would “remain out of the Union one hundred years rather than come in without the women.” It was admitted on July 10, 1890, as the 44th state.
tossups.r: It kept its women’s voting rights and became known as the Equality State. For 10 points, name this state.

tossups.p: During World War II, the Heart Mountain camp in this state held more than 10,000 Japanese Americans at its peak, and some young men there formed the Fair Play Committee to resist being drafted while their families were held in the camp.
tossups.r: The camp stood near Cody, a town named for Buffalo Bill. For 10 points, name this state, home to Yellowstone National Park.

tossups.p: The Green River Basin in this state holds the world’s largest known deposit of trona, a mineral used to make soda ash for glass. Huge open-pit mines in its Powder River Basin have made it the nation’s top coal producer.
tossups.r: Its capital is Cheyenne. For 10 points, name this state, home to Yellowstone and Devils Tower.

tossups.p: James Cash Penney opened his first store, called the Golden Rule, in the mining town of Kemmerer in this state in 1902. This state’s flag shows a white bison, and its license plates feature a cowboy riding a bucking horse.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this state nicknamed both the Cowboy State and the Equality State.

tossups.p: In 1892, wealthy cattle ranchers hired gunmen from Texas to attack small ranchers they accused of stealing cattle in this state’s Johnson County, until President Benjamin Harrison sent in the cavalry.
tossups.r: Butch Cassidy’s gang also hid out at the nearby Hole-in-the-Wall. For 10 points, name this state whose capital is Cheyenne.

tossups.p: This state took its name from a valley in Pennsylvania, using a Lenape [“leh-NAH-pay”] word often translated as “at the big river flat.” A popular 1809 poem by Thomas Campbell had made that valley famous.
tossups.r: Shaped almost like a rectangle, this state borders six others, including Montana and Colorado. For 10 points, name this Rocky Mountain state whose capital is Cheyenne.

trap.title: Which Rocky Mountain state?
trap.body: Wyoming’s neighbors share many of its clues. Montana and Idaho also hold small slices of Yellowstone, Utah Territory let women vote in 1870, just months after Wyoming did, and Colorado is the other state shaped almost like a rectangle. A tossup about the 1778 attack in the Wyoming Valley is about Pennsylvania, not this state.
trap.fix: The Equality State, Cheyenne, Devils Tower, Teapot Dome, Nellie Tayloe Ross, and the 1869 suffrage law all mean Wyoming. Helena, Glacier National Park, or the Little Bighorn mean Montana; Denver or Pikes Peak mean Colorado; Salt Lake City means Utah.

topics.name: XYZ Affair
topics.kicker: French bribery scandal of 1797–1798 · Led to the Quasi-War with France
topics.briefing: In 1797, President John Adams sent three diplomats to Paris to make peace with France, which had been seizing American ships. Agents of the French foreign minister, Talleyrand, told them that talks could not even begin without a large bribe and a loan. When Adams released the diplomats’ reports in 1798, he replaced the agents’ names with the letters X, Y, and Z, and angry Americans cheered, “Millions for defense, but not one cent for tribute!”

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: France refused to receive Charles Cotesworth Pinckney as the American minister in 1796, so in 1797 John Adams sent Pinckney back to Paris with John Marshall and Elbridge Gerry to try to make peace.
tossups.r: French agents told the three men that talks could not begin without a bribe. For 10 points, name this scandal named for three letters.

tossups.p: When a French agent pressed for money, Charles Cotesworth Pinckney reportedly answered, “No, no, not a sixpence!” Pinckney had been sent to Paris along with John Marshall and Elbridge Gerry.
tossups.r: When John Adams later sent their reports to Congress, the French agents’ names were replaced by letters. For 10 points, name this 1797–1798 bribery scandal.

tossups.p: Democratic-Republicans in Congress, expecting proof that John Adams was unfairly hostile to France, demanded to see his diplomats’ reports from Paris. When Adams released them in April 1798, the reports set off a wave of anger against France instead.
tossups.r: Adams had replaced the French agents’ names with letters. For 10 points, name this affair in which those agents demanded a bribe.

tossups.p: At a June 1798 dinner in Philadelphia honoring John Marshall, Congressman Robert Goodloe Harper offered a toast that became a national slogan. Marshall had just returned from a failed peace mission to Paris.
tossups.r: That toast was “Millions for defense, but not one cent for tribute.” For 10 points, name this scandal in which French agents demanded a bribe.

tossups.p: After his two fellow envoys left Paris in 1798, Elbridge Gerry stayed behind, hoping to prevent a war, and angry Federalists accused him of being too friendly to France. Gerry later became James Madison’s vice president.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this scandal in which agents of Talleyrand [“TAL-ee-rand”] demanded a bribe from Gerry, John Marshall, and Charles Cotesworth Pinckney.

tossups.p: In the angry months after this affair became public, Congress created the Department of the Navy, and Benjamin Stoddert became the first secretary of the Navy. Congress also declared the 1778 treaties with France void.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this scandal in which French agents demanded a bribe from American diplomats.

tossups.p: Captain Thomas Truxtun’s frigate _Constellation_ captured the French frigate _L’Insurgente_ [“lan-sur-ZHAHNT”] in 1799, during an undeclared naval war that followed this event. American warships captured dozens of French privateers in that conflict.
tossups.r: That conflict was the Quasi-War. For 10 points, name this 1797–1798 bribery scandal involving the diplomats John Marshall and Elbridge Gerry.

tossups.p: Riding a wave of anger at France after this event, Federalists in Congress passed laws that made it harder to become a citizen and made it a crime to publish “false, scandalous and malicious” writing against the government.
tossups.r: Those laws were the Alien and Sedition Acts. For 10 points, name this affair in which French agents asked American diplomats for a bribe.

tossups.p: The French foreign minister at the center of this scandal later helped sell the Louisiana Territory to the United States and represented France at the Congress of Vienna after Napoleon’s defeat.
tossups.r: His agents had asked American diplomats for a payment of about $250,000. For 10 points, name this 1797–1798 scandal involving Talleyrand [“TAL-ee-rand”].

tossups.p: One diplomat came home from this scandal to a hero’s welcome in Philadelphia in 1798, won a seat in Congress, and became John Adams’s secretary of state before Adams made him Chief Justice in 1801.
tossups.r: That man was John Marshall. For 10 points, name this scandal in which French agents demanded a bribe before they would negotiate.

tossups.p: Oliver Ellsworth, William Davie, and William Vans Murray negotiated the Convention of 1800, which ended the undeclared naval war that broke out after this scandal and formally ended the 1778 alliance with France.
tossups.r: That naval war was the Quasi-War. For 10 points, name this 1797–1798 affair in which agents of Talleyrand [“TAL-ee-rand”] demanded a bribe.

tossups.p: As war with France seemed close after this scandal, John Adams called the retired George Washington back to command a new army, and Washington insisted that Alexander Hamilton be his second-in-command. That army never fought, because the conflict stayed at sea.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this affair in which French agents demanded a bribe from three American diplomats.

tossups.p: The Federalist Party later nominated one diplomat from this scandal for president in 1804 and 1808, though he lost to Thomas Jefferson and then James Madison. That South Carolinian had also signed the Constitution in 1787.
tossups.r: That man was Charles Cotesworth Pinckney. For 10 points, name this 1797–1798 scandal in which French agents demanded a bribe.

tossups.p: French agents in this scandal said their foreign minister expected a douceur [“doo-SUR”], French for a “sweetener.” They also wanted a large loan to France and an apology for a speech by John Adams.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this affair named for the letters that replaced the agents’ names in the reports Adams sent to Congress.

tossups.p: Angry about the Jay Treaty with Britain, France let its privateers seize hundreds of American merchant ships in the mid-1790s. A peace mission that John Adams sent to Paris in 1797 ended in this scandal instead.
tossups.r: Three French agents, later called by letters, had demanded a bribe. For 10 points, name this affair.

trap.title: The scandal, not the war
trap.body: The XYZ Affair (1797–1798) was the bribery scandal. The Quasi-War (1798–1800) was the undeclared naval war it led to, and the Alien and Sedition Acts were laws passed in the same angry months, so all three share clues. The Citizen Genêt affair (1793) was a different clash with France, under George Washington.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun. “This affair,” “this scandal,” or “this incident” with bribes, Talleyrand, or the three envoys wants the XYZ Affair. “This conflict” or “this war” with frigates like the _Constellation_ wants the Quasi-War, and “these laws” wants the Alien and Sedition Acts.
trap.line: Real answer line: XYZ Affair (do not accept “Quasi-War”)

topics.name: 27th Amendment
topics.kicker: Delays congressional pay changes until after an election · Ratified 1992
topics.briefing: The 27th Amendment says that if Congress changes its own pay, the change cannot take effect until after the next election for the House of Representatives. James Madison proposed it in 1789, but it sat unratified for almost two centuries until 1982, when a University of Texas student named Gregory Watson wrote a paper about it, got a C, and started a letter-writing campaign. It was finally ratified in 1992, about 202 years after Congress first proposed it.
topics.answerHtml: Twenty-seventh Amendment (or 27th Amendment or Amendment XXVII; accept Congressional Compensation Amendment; prompt on 27th alone; do not accept other numbers)
reject: district of columbia voting rights amendment

tossups.p: In 1982, a University of Texas student named Gregory Watson wrote a paper arguing that this amendment, which Congress had proposed almost two centuries earlier, could still be ratified. He got a C on the paper and then launched a letter-writing campaign to state lawmakers.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this amendment, ratified in 1992, which delays changes in congressional pay until after the next House election.

tossups.p: When James Madison introduced his proposed amendments in the House in June 1789, he included this one. It was second on the list of twelve that Congress sent to the states that September, just ahead of the amendment protecting freedom of speech.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this amendment about congressional pay, which was finally ratified in 1992.

tossups.p: The word “varying” in this amendment means it covers pay cuts as well as raises. Its single sentence was first proposed by James Madison, who also drafted the amendments that became the Bill of Rights.
tossups.r: It says such a change cannot “take effect, until an election of Representatives shall have intervened.” For 10 points, name this amendment ratified in 1992.

tossups.p: In 1873, Ohio’s legislature approved this long-forgotten amendment to protest the “Salary Grab Act,” under which members of Congress had given themselves a raise along with back pay for the previous two years.
tossups.r: More than a century later, it was finally ratified. For 10 points, name this amendment that delays congressional pay changes until after the next House election.

tossups.p: In 1978, Wyoming’s legislature approved this amendment to protest a congressional pay raise, more than a century after Ohio had done the same thing for the same reason. Four years later, a college student began a national campaign for it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this amendment, first proposed by James Madison, that was ratified in 1992.

tossups.p: No other amendment took nearly as long to ratify as this one, which became part of the Constitution about 202 years after Congress sent it to the states. Because it was proposed long before Congress began setting deadlines for ratification, it never expired.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this amendment, ratified in 1992, that deals with pay raises for members of Congress.

tossups.p: In May 1992, the Archivist of the United States, Don W. Wilson, certified this amendment as ratified, and both houses of Congress then passed resolutions, by lopsided votes, agreeing that it was valid.
tossups.r: A college student’s letter-writing campaign had revived it. For 10 points, name this amendment that delays any congressional pay raise until after the next House election.

tossups.p: Questions about whether this amendment had taken too long to ratify recalled the 1939 case _Coleman v. Miller_, in which the Supreme Court said that Congress, not the courts, decides such questions. An earlier case, _Dillon v. Gloss_, had said amendments should be ratified within a “reasonable time.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this amendment ratified in 1992, about two centuries after James Madison proposed it.

tossups.p: In 2017, the University of Texas changed a grade from a C to an A, decades after a student’s paper about this amendment launched the campaign that got it ratified. That student, Gregory Watson, had written to lawmakers in state after state.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this amendment, ratified in 1992, that delays changes in congressional pay.

tossups.p: Ratified more than twenty years after the amendment that lowered the voting age to 18, this amendment was the only one added to the Constitution in the 1990s. Its idea had first been proposed in 1789.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this amendment that stops a congressional pay raise from taking effect until after the next House election.

tossups.p: Called “Article the Second” in the list Congress sent to the states in 1789, this amendment came right after a proposal about how many people each House member should represent, which has never been ratified.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this amendment about congressional pay, which finally became part of the Constitution in 1992.

tossups.p: Public anger over Congress raising its own pay in the 1980s helped push dozens of state legislatures to approve this amendment, which had sat unratified for nearly two centuries. In May 1992, it reached the 38 states needed for ratification.
tossups.r: It delays congressional pay changes until after a House election. For 10 points, name this amendment first proposed by James Madison.

tossups.p: Article I of the Constitution says members of Congress shall be paid an amount “to be ascertained by law,” which means Congress sets its own salaries. The First Congress paid its members six dollars for each day they attended.
tossups.r: James Madison proposed this amendment so that a pay change would have to wait until after the next House election. For 10 points, name this amendment ratified in 1992.

tossups.p: This amendment was one of two proposals from 1789 that were left out when ten others became the Bill of Rights in 1791. Only a handful of states had approved it by then, and it was nearly forgotten for decades.
tossups.r: It was finally ratified in 1992. For 10 points, name this amendment about congressional pay.

tossups.p: Federal courts ruled that the automatic yearly cost-of-living increases for members of Congress, set up by a 1989 ethics law, do not violate this amendment, which was ratified just a few years after that law passed.
tossups.r: It delays any other change in congressional pay until after the next House election. For 10 points, name this amendment, finally ratified after about 202 years.

trap.title: Get the number right
trap.body: The last few amendments blur together. The 26th Amendment (1971) lowered the voting age to 18, the 25th covers what happens if a president dies or cannot serve, the 22nd limits presidents to two terms, and the 20th moved Inauguration Day to January. Some players also say “Bill of Rights,” because this amendment was proposed in 1789 along with the first ten, but it was not ratified until 1992.
trap.fix: Congressional pay, Gregory Watson, a C on a college paper, 1992, and 202 years all mean the Twenty-seventh Amendment. Say the number clearly. Voting age 18 means the 26th, and two-term limits mean the 22nd.

topics.name: Abolitionism
topics.kicker: The movement to end slavery · Grew into a national crusade in the 1830s
topics.dates: Roots in the late 1600s; a national movement from the 1830s to 1865
topics.briefing: Abolitionism, the movement to end slavery, grew in the 1830s from a few small groups into a national crusade led by people like William Lloyd Garrison, who demanded immediate emancipation in _The Liberator_, and later Frederick Douglass, who had escaped slavery himself. Abolitionists gave speeches, flooded Congress with petitions, and spread books such as _Uncle Tom’s Cabin_. Many faced angry mobs, and in 1837 a mob in Illinois killed the editor Elijah Lovejoy.
topics.answerHtml: abolitionism (or abolitionist movement; accept antislavery movement; prompt on emancipation; do not accept “Underground Railroad,” “Emancipation Proclamation,” or “Free Soil Party”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In November 1837, a proslavery mob in Alton, Illinois, killed the newspaper editor Elijah Lovejoy while he defended his printing press. Weeks later, the young lawyer Wendell Phillips gave his first famous speech for this cause at Boston’s Faneuil Hall, protesting that killing.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this movement, led by William Lloyd Garrison and Frederick Douglass, that demanded freedom for all enslaved people.

tossups.p: Raised in a slaveholding family in Charleston, South Carolina, two sisters moved north and became speakers for this cause. In 1838, the younger sister, Angelina Grimké, became the first woman to address an American legislative body.
tossups.r: She spoke to a committee of the Massachusetts legislature. For 10 points, name this movement that fought to end slavery in the United States.

tossups.p: An antislavery weekly in Washington, D.C., called _The National Era_ first printed a novel in installments in 1851 and 1852, and the book version sold hundreds of thousands of copies. That novel’s characters include Eliza, who escapes across the frozen Ohio River.
tossups.r: That novel, Harriet Beecher Stowe’s _Uncle Tom’s Cabin_, won many Northerners over to this cause. For 10 points, name this movement against slavery.

tossups.p: The wealthy New York merchants Arthur and Lewis Tappan helped pay for a national organization founded in Philadelphia in December 1833 to advance this cause. Its Declaration of Sentiments promised to work without violence.
tossups.r: That group was the American Anti-Slavery Society. For 10 points, name this movement, whose leaders included William Lloyd Garrison.

tossups.p: James G. Birney, a former slaveholder, ran for president in 1840 and 1844 as the candidate of the Liberty Party, the first political party built around this cause. In 1844, Birney’s votes in New York may have cost Henry Clay the election.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this movement, which William Lloyd Garrison led through his newspaper _The Liberator_.

tossups.p: Born Isabella Baumfree in New York, one leader of this cause walked away from slavery in 1826 with her baby daughter and later won a court case to get back her young son, who had been illegally sold to an owner in Alabama.
tossups.r: She later took the name Sojourner Truth. For 10 points, name this movement against slavery.

tossups.p: From 1836 to 1844, the House of Representatives used a “gag rule” to table, without debate, the flood of petitions sent by supporters of this cause. Former president John Quincy Adams fought the rule for years until it was finally repealed.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this movement that worked to end slavery, led by figures like William Lloyd Garrison.

tossups.p: In 1835, supporters of this cause mailed huge numbers of pamphlets to Southern towns, and a mob in Charleston broke into the post office and burned them. Andrew Jackson’s postmaster general allowed Southern postmasters to refuse to deliver such mail.
tossups.r: Its national society organized that mailing campaign. For 10 points, name this movement, which demanded an immediate end to slavery.

tossups.p: In 1829, David Walker, a free Black man in Boston, published an _Appeal_ urging enslaved people to resist, and in 1843 Henry Highland Garnet told a convention, “Let your motto be resistance!” Both men were radical voices in this movement.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this movement against slavery, whose best-known newspaper was William Lloyd Garrison’s _The Liberator_.

tossups.p: In 1834, students at Lane Seminary in Cincinnati held more than two weeks of debates on slavery, and many left for Oberlin College after the school tried to silence them. Their leader, Theodore Weld, later wrote _American Slavery As It Is_ to support this cause.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this movement that demanded the freeing of all enslaved people.

tossups.p: In 1688, four Quakers in Germantown, Pennsylvania, signed one of the earliest written protests against slavery in the colonies. Later Quakers such as John Woolman and Anthony Benezet [“BEN-uh-zet”] carried on this cause, and Benjamin Franklin led a Pennsylvania society devoted to it.
tossups.r: The cause grew into a national movement in the 1830s. For 10 points, name this movement against slavery.

tossups.p: Josiah Wedgwood’s factory made a medallion showing a kneeling, chained man who asks, “Am I Not a Man and a Brother?” It became a symbol of this cause, which in Britain was led by William Wilberforce and won an 1833 law ending slavery in most of the empire.
tossups.r: In the United States, its leaders included Frederick Douglass. For 10 points, name this movement against slavery.

tossups.p: When women delegates were shut out of a world convention for this cause in London in 1840, Lucretia Mott and Elizabeth Cady Stanton met and decided that women needed their own movement. Eight years later, they organized the Seneca Falls Convention.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this movement against slavery that helped launch the fight for women’s rights.

tossups.p: Lewis Tappan organized a committee to defend the Africans who had seized the Spanish schooner _Amistad_ in 1839, and former president John Quincy Adams argued their case before the Supreme Court, which freed them in 1841.
tossups.r: Tappan also helped found the American Anti-Slavery Society. For 10 points, name this movement against slavery led by people like William Lloyd Garrison.

tossups.p: Founded in Philadelphia in 1833, the national society of this movement voted to disband in 1870, after the Fifteenth Amendment protected Black men’s right to vote. Wendell Phillips had led that society for its last five years.
tossups.r: The movement’s best-known newspaper had stopped printing in 1865, once the Thirteenth Amendment ended slavery. For 10 points, name this movement led by William Lloyd Garrison and Frederick Douglass.

trap.title: The movement, not a person
trap.body: Tossups on this movement are full of names, and William Lloyd Garrison, Frederick Douglass, Harriet Tubman, and Sojourner Truth all have their own answer lines, so naming one of them is wrong when the question asks for “this movement.” The Underground Railroad (the escape network), the Emancipation Proclamation (Lincoln’s 1863 order), and the Free Soil Party (an 1848 party against spreading slavery west) are separate answers too.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun. “This movement,” “this cause,” or “this crusade” wants abolitionism (“abolition” is fine). “This network” means the Underground Railroad, “this party” could mean the Liberty or Free Soil Party, and “this man” or “this woman” wants a person.

topics.name: Affirmative action
topics.kicker: Programs to widen opportunity for minorities and women · Begun in the 1960s
topics.briefing: Affirmative action means taking active steps to widen opportunities in jobs, contracts, and college admissions for groups that have faced discrimination, such as racial minorities and women. Presidents John F. Kennedy and Lyndon Johnson started federal programs in the 1960s, and in 2023 the Supreme Court ruled that colleges may not use race-conscious admissions programs. Supporters argue it makes up for past and present discrimination and builds diversity; opponents argue it treats people unequally because of race or sex.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In March 1961, John F. Kennedy’s Executive Order 10925 told government contractors to make sure job applicants were treated “without regard to their race, creed, color, or national origin.” That order created a committee on equal job opportunity led by Vice President Lyndon Johnson.
tossups.r: Kennedy’s order called for this policy by name. For 10 points, name this policy of taking active steps to open jobs and schools to groups that faced discrimination.

tossups.p: Lyndon Johnson’s Executive Order 11246, signed in September 1965, required companies with federal contracts to take active steps against job discrimination and put the Labor Department in charge of enforcing it. A 1967 order added discrimination based on sex.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this policy, which aims to widen opportunities for women and minorities and was tested in court cases such as _Regents v. Bakke_.

tossups.p: In a 1965 speech at Howard University, Lyndon Johnson argued that it was not enough to free a person who had been held back for years, bring him to the starting line of a race, and then say he was free to compete.
tossups.r: Opponents of this policy argue that it treats people unequally because of race. For 10 points, name this policy, ended in college admissions by a 2023 Supreme Court ruling.

tossups.p: In 1969, the Labor Department under Secretary George Shultz put the Philadelphia Plan into effect, requiring construction companies on federally funded projects in that city to set goals and timetables for hiring minority workers in skilled trades.
tossups.r: That plan under Richard Nixon was an early example of this policy. For 10 points, name this policy, which the Supreme Court addressed in the _Bakke_ case.

tossups.p: A white applicant who was rejected twice by the medical school at the University of California, Davis, sued because the school set aside 16 of its 100 places for minority students. In 1978, the Supreme Court ruled 5–4 that this fixed quota was not allowed and ordered him admitted.
tossups.r: But in _Regents v. Bakke_, Justice Lewis Powell wrote that race could be one factor among many. For 10 points, name this policy that the case limited but did not end.

tossups.p: In _United Steelworkers v. Weber_ (1979), the Supreme Court upheld a training program at a Kaiser Aluminum plant that saved half its spots for Black workers. A year later, _Fullilove v. Klutznick_ upheld a federal law setting aside some public works money for minority-owned businesses.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this kind of policy, which tries to widen opportunities for groups that faced discrimination.

tossups.p: In _City of Richmond v. J.A. Croson Co._ (1989), the Supreme Court struck down a Virginia city’s rule setting aside 30 percent of construction contract money for minority-owned businesses. Six years later, _Adarand Constructors v. Peña_ [“PAYN-yuh”] said federal programs that use race must pass “strict scrutiny.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this kind of policy, which considers race or sex to widen opportunities.

tossups.p: In a campaign led by the businessman Ward Connerly, California voters approved Proposition 209 in 1996, banning state agencies and public universities from giving preference to anyone based on race, sex, or ethnicity. In 2020, voters rejected a measure that would have repealed it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this policy that Proposition 209 ended in California’s public colleges and government jobs.

tossups.p: After a federal court ruled in _Hopwood v. Texas_ (1996) that the University of Texas law school could not consider race, Texas guaranteed admission to its public universities for students in the top ten percent of their high school classes. Abigail Fisher later challenged the university’s use of race.
tossups.r: In 2016, the Supreme Court upheld the Texas program 4–3. For 10 points, name this policy, often called race-conscious admissions.

tossups.p: In _Gratz v. Bollinger_ (2003), the Supreme Court struck down the University of Michigan’s undergraduate admissions system, which automatically gave 20 points out of 150 to applicants from underrepresented minority groups.
tossups.r: On the same day, a related case upheld a more flexible plan at Michigan’s law school. For 10 points, name this policy that both cases tested.

tossups.p: Writing for a 5–4 majority in _Grutter v. Bollinger_ (2003), Justice Sandra Day O’Connor upheld the University of Michigan Law School’s use of race as one factor and wrote that she expected it to be unnecessary “25 years from now.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this policy that a 2023 Supreme Court ruling ended in college admissions.

tossups.p: Edward Blum founded a group that sued Harvard and the University of North Carolina over how they chose students. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson sat out the Harvard case because she had served on one of Harvard’s governing boards.
tossups.r: In June 2023, the Supreme Court ruled for that group, Students for Fair Admissions. For 10 points, name this policy that the ruling ended in college admissions.

tossups.p: In 2006, Michigan voters approved Proposal 2, which banned public colleges in that state from giving preference based on race or sex. In 2014, the Supreme Court upheld that ban in a case named for Michigan’s attorney general, Bill Schuette [“SHOO-tee”].
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this policy, which California had also banned in public colleges with Proposition 209.

tossups.p: In January 2025, President Donald Trump signed an order revoking Executive Order 11246, which for about sixty years had required federal contractors to take active steps against job discrimination.
tossups.r: Lyndon Johnson had signed that order in 1965. For 10 points, name this policy, which the Supreme Court had ended in college admissions in 2023.

tossups.p: A footnote in one Supreme Court opinion set aside the question of the military academies, and the opinion said colleges could still consider an applicant’s essay about how race had affected his or her life.
tossups.r: Chief Justice John Roberts wrote that 2023 opinion, which ended race-conscious college admissions. For 10 points, name this policy that _Grutter v. Bollinger_ had upheld in 2003.

trap.title: Policy, not law or clause
trap.body: Tossups on this policy mention several related answer lines. The Civil Rights Act of 1964 banned discrimination in jobs and public places, the Equal Protection Clause of the 14th Amendment is the part of the Constitution courts used to judge these programs, and _Brown v. Board of Education_ (1954) ended legal school segregation. Naming one of them is wrong when the question asks for “this policy.”
trap.fix: Executive Orders 10925 and 11246, _Bakke_, _Gratz_, _Grutter_, Proposition 209, and _Students for Fair Admissions_ all point to affirmative action. If the question asks for “this clause,” say Equal Protection; if it asks for “this law” from 1964, say the Civil Rights Act.
trap.line: Real answer line: affirmative action (prompt on descriptions like race-conscious admissions)

topics.name: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez
topics.kicker: U.S. Representative from New York, first elected in 2018 · Known as AOC
topics.briefing: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez grew up in New York, graduated from Boston University, and was working as a bartender when she ran for Congress. In a 2018 Democratic primary, she defeated Joe Crowley, a ten-term congressman and party leader, and that November, at 29, she won the seat for New York’s 14th district, in the Bronx and Queens, becoming the youngest woman elected to Congress up to that time. A self-described democratic socialist, she is widely known as AOC.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: As a high school student, this future politician won second prize in microbiology at the 2007 Intel International Science and Engineering Fair, and a small asteroid was later named after her. She went on to study economics and international relations at Boston University.
tossups.r: In 2018, she was elected to Congress from New York at age 29. For 10 points, name this congresswoman widely known by her initials.

tossups.p: While in college, this future lawmaker worked as an intern on immigration issues for Senator Ted Kennedy. After graduating, she worked as a bartender and waitress in Manhattan to help support her family.
tossups.r: In 2018, she defeated Joe Crowley in a Democratic primary. For 10 points, name this congresswoman from the Bronx and Queens.

tossups.p: After visiting the protests against the Dakota Access Pipeline at Standing Rock in December 2016, this organizer decided to run for office, and the group Justice Democrats backed her campaign. She had earlier worked as an organizer for Bernie Sanders’s 2016 presidential campaign.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this democratic socialist who was elected to the House from New York in 2018.

tossups.p: In a June 2018 primary, this first-time candidate defeated Joe Crowley, the chairman of the House Democratic Caucus, who had represented his district for ten terms. Her win, by about 57 percent to 43 percent, surprised many political observers.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this New York congresswoman who that November became the youngest woman elected to Congress up to that time.

tossups.p: In February 2019, this freshman representative and Senator Ed Markey of Massachusetts introduced a nonbinding resolution calling for a fast national shift to clean energy to fight climate change, along with new jobs programs. Its name recalls Franklin Roosevelt’s programs of the 1930s.
tossups.r: That resolution was the Green New Deal. For 10 points, name this New York congresswoman, a self-described democratic socialist.

tossups.p: This congresswoman, Ilhan Omar of Minnesota, Rashida Tlaib of Michigan, and Ayanna Pressley of Massachusetts were all first elected to the House in 2018, and all four were Democratic women of color.
tossups.r: The four became widely known as “the Squad.” For 10 points, name this Squad member who won a House seat representing parts of the Bronx and Queens.

tossups.p: Rachel Lears’s documentary _Knock Down the House_, which premiered at the Sundance Film Festival and was released on Netflix in 2019, followed four women who ran in 2018 Democratic primaries for Congress. This candidate was the only one of the four to win that year.
tossups.r: She defeated Joe Crowley in a primary that June. For 10 points, name this congresswoman from New York.

tossups.p: In October 2020, this congresswoman drew hundreds of thousands of viewers when she played the video game _Among Us_ live on Twitch with Ilhan Omar to encourage people to vote. Months earlier, she gave a short speech at the Democratic National Convention seconding Bernie Sanders’s nomination.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this New York Democrat who was first elected to the House in 2018 at age 29.

tossups.p: In August 2024, this politician spoke at the Democratic National Convention in Chicago. A member of the Democratic Socialists of America, she won reelection to the House in 2020, 2022, and 2024.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this congresswoman who first won her New York seat in 2018 at age 29.

tossups.p: Born in the Bronx in 1989 to a mother from Puerto Rico, this future politician moved as a child to Yorktown Heights in suburban Westchester County. She later returned to the Bronx after college.
tossups.r: In 2018, she won a seat in Congress representing parts of the Bronx and Queens. For 10 points, name this New York Democrat.

tossups.p: When she won her House race in November 2018, this 29-year-old broke a record that Elise Stefanik, a Republican from New York, had set four years earlier. She took office in January 2019, at the start of the 116th Congress.
tossups.r: That record was for the youngest woman ever elected to Congress. For 10 points, name this congresswoman from New York’s 14th district, who had defeated Joe Crowley.

tossups.p: As a member of the House Financial Services Committee, this representative questioned Facebook’s Mark Zuckerberg in 2019 about whether his company would fact-check political ads. Earlier that year, on the House Oversight Committee, she questioned Michael Cohen, Donald Trump’s former lawyer.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this New York congresswoman, first elected in 2018 as one of the four members of “the Squad.”

tossups.p: In a January 2019 interview with Anderson Cooper on _60 Minutes_, this newly sworn-in member of Congress suggested a top tax rate as high as 70 percent on income above $10 million a year.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this democratic socialist from New York who had become the youngest woman elected to Congress up to that time.

tossups.p: In the 2020 Democratic primary, this first-term representative defeated the former CNBC anchor Michelle Caruso-Cabrera [“kuh-ROO-soh kuh-BRAIR-uh”] by a wide margin, and that November she won a second term in the House.
tossups.r: She had first won her seat in 2018 by defeating Joe Crowley. For 10 points, name this New York Democrat, a self-described democratic socialist.

tossups.p: This politician became known for answering questions from followers in live videos on Instagram, sometimes while cooking in her kitchen. In a February 2019 House hearing, she posed a “lightning round” to show how campaign finance rules work, and the video spread widely online.
tossups.r: She had defeated Joe Crowley in a 2018 primary. For 10 points, name this congresswoman from the Bronx and Queens.

trap.body: Four Democratic congresswomen first elected in 2018 became known as “the Squad,” so clues about the group can also fit Ilhan Omar of Minnesota, Rashida Tlaib of Michigan, or Ayanna Pressley of Massachusetts. Elise Stefanik, a Republican from New York, held the record as the youngest woman elected to Congress until Ocasio-Cortez broke it in 2018.

topics.name: Appalachian Mountains
topics.kicker: Ancient range of eastern North America · Boone’s frontier and a famous trail
topics.dates: Began forming over 400 million years ago
topics.briefing: The Appalachian Mountains are some of the oldest mountains on Earth, rounded by hundreds of millions of years of erosion, and they stretch from Alabama to Newfoundland. The Proclamation of 1763 banned colonists from settling west of them, but pioneers like Daniel Boone soon pushed through the Cumberland Gap. Hikers can follow the Appalachian Trail all the way from Georgia to Maine, and Mount Mitchell in North Carolina is the highest peak east of the Mississippi River.
topics.answerHtml: Appalachian Mountains (or Appalachians; prompt on Appalachia; do not accept smaller ranges such as the “Blue Ridge” or “Great Smoky Mountains”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Thomas Clingman argued with a University of North Carolina professor over who had first measured the tallest peak in this range. That professor died in a fall on the mountain in 1857 while checking his measurements, and he is buried on the summit of the peak later named for him.
tossups.r: That peak, Mount Mitchell, is the highest point east of the Mississippi River. For 10 points, name this mountain range of eastern North America.

tossups.p: Forester Benton MacKaye [“muh-KYE”] proposed a long footpath along this range in a 1921 article, and Myron Avery led the effort that completed it in 1937. Avery also became the first person to hike that path’s whole length, one section at a time.
tossups.r: That trail runs from Springer Mountain in Georgia to Mount Katahdin [“kuh-TAH-din”] in Maine. For 10 points, name this mountain range.

tossups.p: In 1955, a 67-year-old grandmother from Ohio named Emma Gatewood became the first woman to hike the full length of a trail along this range by herself. Seven years earlier, Earl Shaffer had become the first person to report hiking that whole trail in a single trip.
tossups.r: Hikers on that trail follow white paint marks from Georgia to Maine. For 10 points, name this mountain range.

tossups.p: In his famous 1893 essay on the frontier, Frederick Jackson Turner told readers to “stand at Cumberland Gap and watch the procession of civilization, marching single file” through this range. He pictured buffalo, Native Americans, fur traders, and pioneer farmers passing through that gap in turn.
tossups.r: Daniel Boone’s Wilderness Road crossed that gap into Kentucky. For 10 points, name these mountains, which the Proclamation of 1763 made the limit of colonial settlement.

tossups.p: Weather observers on the summit of Mount Washington, in this range’s White Mountains, measured a wind gust of 231 miles per hour in 1934, a world record for more than sixty years. A cog railway has carried visitors up that New Hampshire peak since 1869.
tossups.r: This range’s highest peak, though, is Mount Mitchell in North Carolina. For 10 points, name this range that stretches from Alabama to Newfoundland.

tossups.p: The Caledonides of Scotland and the Atlas Mountains of Morocco share matching rocks with this range, because all three were once part of one mountain chain raised as landmasses collided to form the supercontinent Pangaea. Hundreds of millions of years of erosion have worn this range’s once-taller peaks into rounded ridges.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this range in the eastern United States, among the oldest mountains on Earth.

tossups.p: In 1921, thousands of armed coal miners clashed with company-backed forces at the Battle of Blair Mountain in West Virginia until federal troops arrived. Many miners in this range lived in company towns and were paid in scrip, which could be spent only at company stores.
tossups.r: Coal mining long ruled the economy of this range’s hill country. For 10 points, name this range that runs through West Virginia and Kentucky.

tossups.p: Aaron Copland won a Pulitzer Prize for a 1944 ballet whose title names springtime in these mountains; he wrote it for the dancer Martha Graham. That ballet’s music borrows the Shaker hymn “Simple Gifts.”
tossups.r: The fiddle and banjo music of this range’s hill country helped give rise to bluegrass. For 10 points, name this eastern mountain range.

tossups.p: In 1964, Lyndon Johnson visited the home of an unemployed father of eight in Inez, Kentucky, to draw attention to his War on Poverty. A year later, Congress created a regional commission, named for this range, to build roads and fight poverty in the communities along it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this range of the eastern United States, whose highest peak is Mount Mitchell.

tossups.p: A bluish haze, formed partly from chemicals released by trees, gave one part of this range its name. That part’s Clingmans Dome, the highest point in Tennessee, is also the highest point on a famous long-distance hiking trail.
tossups.r: That part, the Great Smoky Mountains, is home to the most visited U.S. national park. For 10 points, name this larger range.

tossups.p: Work on a 469-mile scenic road along this range began in 1935 and was not finished until 1987, when its last section opened on the curving Linn Cove Viaduct around Grandfather Mountain.
tossups.r: That road, the Blue Ridge Parkway, links Shenandoah and Great Smoky Mountains National Parks. For 10 points, name this eastern mountain range.

tossups.p: In 1927, producer Ralph Peer recorded the Carter Family in Bristol, on the Tennessee–Virginia line, in sessions often called the “big bang” of country music. Decades later, Loretta Lynn sang about her childhood in Butcher Hollow, Kentucky, in “Coal Miner’s Daughter.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this mountain range, whose folk music shaped both country and bluegrass.

tossups.p: The Erie Canal followed the valley of the Mohawk River, one of the few low gaps through this range, which gave New York a cheaper route to the Great Lakes than cities farther south had.
tossups.r: Earlier, the Proclamation of 1763 had banned colonists from settling west of this range. For 10 points, name these mountains.

tossups.p: Bill Bryson’s 1998 book _A Walk in the Woods_ describes his attempt to hike a trail along this range. That trail passes through fourteen states, with its longest stretch in Virginia, and its headquarters are in Harpers Ferry, West Virginia.
tossups.r: That trail runs from Georgia to Maine. For 10 points, name this mountain range.

tossups.p: Geologists usually treat New York’s Adirondack Mountains as a separate range from this one, which began forming more than 400 million years ago and has been worn down by erosion ever since.
tossups.r: Its smaller ranges include the Blue Ridge and the Alleghenies. For 10 points, name this range, one of the oldest on Earth.

trap.title: Whole range, not a piece
trap.body: Many famous mountains belong to this one long range: the Blue Ridge, the Great Smoky Mountains, the Alleghenies, the Catskills, and the Green and White Mountains. When a tossup asks for “this range” but clues one of those smaller pieces, answering the piece is wrong. Players also blurt out the Rocky Mountains of the West, or New York’s Adirondacks, which geologists treat as a separate range.
trap.fix: Mount Mitchell, the Proclamation of 1763, Daniel Boone’s Cumberland Gap, coal country, and a trail from Georgia to Maine all mean the Appalachians. Name a smaller range only when the question asks for “this part” of the mountains.
trap.line: Real answer line: Appalachian Mountains (or Appalachians; prompt on Appalachia; do not accept smaller ranges such as the “Blue Ridge” or “Great Smoky Mountains”)

topics.name: Area 51
topics.kicker: Secret Air Force test site in Nevada · Spy planes, stealth jets, UFO legends
topics.briefing: Out in the Nevada desert, beside a dry lakebed called Groom Lake, sits a base so secret that the U.S. government did not openly acknowledge it for decades. Starting in 1955, the CIA tested the U-2 spy plane there; later came the A-12 and stealth jets. All that secrecy made Area 51 the star of countless stories about UFOs and aliens, though no evidence supports them.
topics.answerHtml: Area 51 (accept Homey Airport; prompt on Groom Lake or Nevada; do not accept “Roswell”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: This site was once code-named “Watertown,” after the New York birthplace of CIA director Allen Dulles. Richard Bissell, who later planned the Bay of Pigs invasion, ran Project Aquatone, the secret CIA program that first used this site.
tossups.r: Starting in 1955, the CIA and Lockheed tested the U-2 spy plane here. For 10 points, name this secret base in Nevada, famous in UFO stories.

tossups.p: Clarence “Kelly” Johnson, the head of Lockheed’s secret Skunk Works design team, jokingly nicknamed this lonely desert site “Paradise Ranch” to help persuade workers to move there. His team designed the planes that the CIA tested there.
tossups.r: Beginning in 1955, the U-2 spy plane was tested here. For 10 points, name this secret base at Groom Lake, Nevada.

tossups.p: A plane first tested at this site was shot down over the Soviet Union in 1960, and its pilot, Francis Gary Powers, was captured. Powers was later traded for a Soviet spy.
tossups.r: That plane was the U-2. For 10 points, name this secret Nevada base, which many UFO stories claim is hiding alien spacecraft.

tossups.p: After a Freedom of Information Act request by the National Security Archive, the CIA released a history of its spy-plane programs in 2013 that openly acknowledged this site. The history described how the agency and Lockheed had picked it in 1955.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this secret base at Groom Lake, Nevada, the subject of many UFO conspiracy theories.

tossups.p: According to a declassified CIA history, airline pilots in the 1950s who saw sunlight glinting off a silver plane flying far above them often reported strange objects in the sky. That plane was secretly being tested at this site.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Nevada base, whose secrecy has fueled popular stories about UFOs and aliens.

tossups.p: In the early 1960s, the CIA tested the A-12, a titanium spy plane code-named OXCART, at this site. The A-12 led to the SR-71 Blackbird, which could fly more than three times the speed of sound.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this secret Air Force facility in Nevada, the subject of many UFO legends.

tossups.p: A small stealth test plane called Have Blue first flew at this site in 1977, leading to the F-117 Nighthawk, a jet designed to be very hard to detect by radar. The government kept the F-117 secret until 1988.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Nevada base where secret aircraft are tested, the subject of many UFO stories.

tossups.p: During the Cold War, American pilots secretly test-flew captured Soviet-built MiG fighter jets at this site to learn how to beat them in combat. Some of those jets had reached the West when their pilots defected.
tossups.r: Other secret planes, like the U-2, were also tested here. For 10 points, name this secret base near Groom Lake, Nevada.

tossups.p: In 1996, Nevada officially named State Route 375 the “Extraterrestrial Highway” because it runs near this site. Along that road, the tiny town of Rachel welcomes tourists drawn by stories about this site.
tossups.r: Rachel’s diner and motel have a UFO theme. For 10 points, name this secret Air Force base in Nevada, a favorite subject of UFO believers.

tossups.p: In 2019, a joke Facebook event invited people to rush this site’s gates on September 20, and more than two million users clicked that they were “going.” In the end, only a small crowd showed up, and music festivals sprang up in nearby desert towns.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this secret base in Nevada, which the event jokingly claimed was hiding aliens.

tossups.p: In 1989, a man named Bob Lazar told a Las Vegas TV station that he had worked on secret projects at a site called S-4 near this base, but no evidence has ever supported his story.
tossups.r: Lazar said those projects involved alien spacecraft, one of many UFO stories tied to this place. For 10 points, name this secret Air Force facility north of Las Vegas.

tossups.p: In the 1996 movie _Independence Day_, the U.S. president learns that a spacecraft that crashed decades earlier has been studied in secret inside an underground lab at this real place.
tossups.r: This real base appears in many stories about UFOs. For 10 points, name this secret Air Force facility in Nevada.

tossups.p: Although some people claim that wreckage from a 1947 crash near Roswell, New Mexico, was brought to this site, this site was not set up until 1955. The Air Force later said the Roswell debris came from a secret balloon project.
tossups.r: This base’s real job was testing secret aircraft such as the U-2. For 10 points, name this secret base at Groom Lake, Nevada.

tossups.p: This facility lies in Lincoln County, inside a huge military training range whose airspace is closed to ordinary planes, and many of its workers commute from Las Vegas aboard unmarked passenger jets known by the radio call sign “Janet.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this secret base by Groom Lake, Nevada, famous in UFO stories.

tossups.p: Lockheed test pilot Tony LeVier flew over the Nevada desert looking for a hidden place to test a new plane, and he recommended the dry lakebed at this site. In August 1955, LeVier made the first flights of that plane there.
tossups.r: That plane was the U-2. For 10 points, name this secret base, famous in UFO stories.

trap.title: Not Roswell!
trap.body: UFO stories often tie this base to the 1947 Roswell incident, but Roswell is a town in New Mexico near where debris was found that the Air Force later said came from a secret balloon project, and the base in Nevada was not set up until 1955. Saying “Roswell” loses the tossup. Also, Groom Lake is the dry lakebed beside the base, so naming it earns only a prompt here.
trap.fix: Nevada, Groom Lake, the U-2, the A-12, stealth jets, and the 2019 “storm” event mean Area 51; New Mexico and a 1947 crash mean Roswell. If you are prompted after saying “Groom Lake,” say “Area 51.”

topics.name: Arlington National Cemetery
topics.kicker: Military cemetery on Robert E. Lee’s old estate · Tomb of the Unknown Soldier
topics.briefing: Arlington National Cemetery covers a Virginia hillside that once belonged to Robert E. Lee’s family, across the Potomac River from Washington, D.C. During the Civil War, Union Quartermaster General Montgomery Meigs began burying soldiers there in 1864. More than 400,000 people rest there, including President John F. Kennedy beneath an eternal flame, and soldiers of the Old Guard watch over the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier day and night.
topics.answerHtml: Arlington National Cemetery (accept Arlington Cemetery; prompt on Arlington or Arlington County; do not accept “Arlington House”)
reject: national memorial cemetery of the pacific

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: George Washington Parke Custis, the grandson of Martha Washington, built a Greek Revival mansion on this site partly as a memorial to George Washington. In 1831, Custis’s daughter Mary married a young army officer in that house, and the couple made it their home for about thirty years.
tossups.r: That officer was Robert E. Lee. For 10 points, name this national cemetery created on Lee’s estate in Virginia.

tossups.p: Private William Christman of the 67th Pennsylvania Infantry became the first soldier buried at this site, on May 13, 1864. About a month later, Secretary of War Edwin Stanton approved Quartermaster General Montgomery Meigs’s plan to turn the land into a military cemetery.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this cemetery in Virginia, where the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier stands.

tossups.p: Montgomery Meigs had graves dug close to a mansion on this site, even in its rose garden, reportedly so that the family who had lived there could never move back. Meigs, who was born in Georgia but stayed loyal to the Union, was later buried here himself.
tossups.r: That mansion had been the home of Robert E. Lee. For 10 points, name this military cemetery across the Potomac River from Washington, D.C.

tossups.p: In the 1882 case _United States v. Lee_, the Supreme Court ruled that the federal government had taken this site illegally during the Civil War. The next year, the government paid 150,000 dollars to the family’s eldest son, who had brought the suit, so that it could keep the land.
tossups.r: That son’s father was Robert E. Lee. For 10 points, name this national cemetery on Lee’s former estate.

tossups.p: In 1863, the government set up Freedman’s Village on this estate as a community for formerly enslaved people who had escaped to Union lines. Thousands of freedpeople, along with soldiers of the U.S. Colored Troops, were later buried here.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this cemetery in Virginia, where President John F. Kennedy is buried under an eternal flame.

tossups.p: In 1921, Sergeant Edward Younger walked among four identical caskets in a French city hall and placed white roses on one of them. The soldier in that casket was buried at this site on November 11, 1921, in a ceremony led by President Warren G. Harding.
tossups.r: That soldier lies in the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier. For 10 points, name this cemetery across the Potomac River from Washington, D.C.

tossups.p: In 1998, DNA tests identified the remains in one crypt at this site as those of Air Force pilot Michael Blassie, who had been shot down in Vietnam, and that crypt has been left empty ever since.
tossups.r: Unknowns from World War II and Korea had been placed at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier in 1958. For 10 points, name this national cemetery in Virginia.

tossups.p: Soldiers from the 3rd U.S. Infantry Regiment, nicknamed “The Old Guard,” keep watch over a memorial at this site, which has been guarded every hour of every day since 1937. Each sentinel takes 21 steps and then pauses for 21 seconds, recalling a 21-gun salute.
tossups.r: That memorial is the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier. For 10 points, name this cemetery on Robert E. Lee’s former estate.

tossups.p: The marble for a famous tomb at this site, finished in 1932, came from the same Colorado quarry that supplied the outer marble of the Lincoln Memorial. One side of that tomb reads “Here rests in honored glory an American soldier known but to God.”
tossups.r: That tomb holds the Unknown Soldier from World War I. For 10 points, name this national cemetery in Virginia.

tossups.p: Only two U.S. presidents are buried at this site. One of them, William Howard Taft, is the only person to have served as both president and Chief Justice of the United States.
tossups.r: The other, John F. Kennedy, lies beneath an eternal flame that his widow lit at his 1963 funeral. For 10 points, name this cemetery.

tossups.p: In 1909, the remains of Pierre L’Enfant [“lahn-FAHN”] were moved to this site and reburied on a hillside overlooking the capital city he had planned. L’Enfant had been fired in 1792 and died poor.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this cemetery in Virginia, home of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier and the grave of John F. Kennedy.

tossups.p: Abraham Lincoln’s son Robert Todd Lincoln is buried at this site rather than with his parents in Springfield, Illinois. Boxing champion Joe Louis and civil rights leader Medgar Evers, both World War II veterans, are also buried here.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this military cemetery where John F. Kennedy is buried under an eternal flame.

tossups.p: A bridge opened in 1932 across the Potomac River links the Lincoln Memorial to this site, symbolizing the North and South reunited after the Civil War. The Women in Military Service for America Memorial, dedicated in 1997, stands at this site’s ceremonial entrance.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this cemetery on Robert E. Lee’s former estate, home of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier.

tossups.p: Memorials at this site honor the crews lost aboard the space shuttles _Challenger_ in 1986 and _Columbia_ in 2003. The mast of the battleship USS _Maine_, which sank in Havana harbor in 1898, also stands here.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this national cemetery in Virginia, where the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier stands.

tossups.p: Unlike most national cemeteries, which are run by the Department of Veterans Affairs, this one is run by the U.S. Army. More than 400,000 people are buried at this site, and military funerals are held here almost every weekday.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this cemetery across the Potomac River from Washington, D.C., where John F. Kennedy is buried.
